notes.short: One prophet of the LORD against Baal's 450
notes.about: Elijah stands alone on Carmel, calling himself “the only remaining prophet of the LORD,” against Baal's 450. They shout, leap and cut themselves from morning to evening, and no one answers. Many also set his one short, calm prayer against their cries. Then the fire of the LORD falls.

sides.label: One prophet, one short prayer
sides.words: I am the only remaining prophet of the LORD

sides.label: Many, crying out all day unanswered
sides.words: they kept on raving until the time of the evening sacrifice

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry: Baal's cause had 450 men, God's but one; Elijah's short, calm prayer was far from their frenzy. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes): Elijah sets his lone stand against the crowd. Alfred Barry (Ellicott's Commentary): their wild cry stands against Elijah's simple prayer. Alexander Maclaren: alone, Elijah towers above the crowd; his calm prayer is in sharp contrast with their cries.
notes.limit: He was not the only one left who was faithful: Obadiah had hidden a hundred prophets of the LORD, and God kept seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed to Baal.

cites.quote: The managers of Baal's cause were 450 men, fat and well fed ... The manager of God's cause was but one man, lately a poor exile, hardly kept from starving ... His prayer was not long, for he used no vain repetitions ... but it was very grave and composed, and showed his mind to be calm and sedate, and far from the heats and disorders that Baal's prophets were in
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The others ... had been forced to fly and hide themselves in dens and caves of the earth; their voices were silenced; they had not ventured to come to Carmel. Elijah contrasts his solitary appearance on the side of Yahweh at the great gathering with the crowd of those opposed to him.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This repeated cry ... uttered probably first in measured chant, afterwards in a wild excited cry ... stands in an instructive contrast ... with the simple, earnest solemnity of the prayer of Elijah.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: Then Elijah takes the command, and, though utterly alone, towers above the crowd in the courage of his undaunted confidence in his message ... The tranquil though earnest prayer of the prophet is in sharpest contrast with the meaningless bellowings to Baal.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/maclaren/1_kings/18.htm

notes.short: Elijah's taunt: “Shout louder, for he is a god!”
notes.about: Elijah taunts the prophets of Baal: shout louder, for he is a god, perhaps lost in thought, busy, travelling or asleep. He means the opposite. Baal does not answer because he is no god, and the taunt drives them on until all can see that no one answered (verse 29).

figure.name: Irony
figure.words: Shout louder, for he is a god!
figure.means: that Baal is no god at all, since he cannot hear or answer however loud they cry

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the words under Irony as sarcasm of the severest kind. Adam Clarke calls them a strong irony, and Robert Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says Elijah exposed their folly with the severest irony. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) says the irony spurred the priests on, so that failure would prove Baal no God. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) hears derision: a god in their opinion only.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Human Irony, p. 813
cites.quote: The words of Elijah to the prophets of Baal were sarcasm of the severest kind.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: he is the supreme God, you worship him as such, he must needs be such, and no doubt jealous of his own honor and the credit of his votaries! A strong irony.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: No response was heard. No fire descended. Elijah exposed their folly and imposture with the severest irony
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The object of Elijah's irony was two-fold; (1) to stimulate the priests to greater exertions, and so to make their failure more complete, and (2) to suggest to the people that such failure would prove absolutely that Baal was no God.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As no answer had been received before noon, Elijah cried out to them in derision ... for he is God (sc., according to your opinion) ... The ridicule lies more especially in the ... (for he is a god), when contrasted with the enumeration of the different possibilities which may have occasioned their obtaining no answer
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Micaiah echoes the false prophets in mockery
notes.about: Micaiah answers with the same promise the king's prophets gave (verse 12), but he means the opposite, and Ahab hears it: he makes him swear to tell only the truth (verse 16). Then Micaiah tells what he saw, Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd.

figure.name: Irony
figure.means: that Ahab will not triumph: Micaiah mocks the promise of the king's false prophets

original.note: In Hebrew Micaiah's answer repeats the prophets' words in verse 12, with the same verbs for “go up” and “prosper”; the BSB says “triumph” here.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the answer under Irony, showing up the false prophecies of Ahab's own prophets. Adam Clarke calls it a strong irony. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) and Robert Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) say Micaiah used the prophets' words in a mocking, ironical tone, and Matthew Henry that he spoke as they had, but ironically.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Human Irony, p. 813
cites.quote: The words of the prophet Micaiah to Ahab and Jehoshaphat: “Go, and prosper”; to show by Irony the false prophecies of Ahab’s own prophets.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This was a strong irony; as if he had said, All your prophets have predicted success; you wish me to speak as they speak ... spoken by Micaiah in such a tone and manner as at once showed to Ahab that he did not believe them
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Micaiah speaks the exact words of the 400 in so mocking and ironical a tone, that the king cannot mistake his meaning, or regard his answer as serious.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: the prophet gave precisely the same answer as the previous oracles that had been consulted; but it must have been given in a sarcastic tone and in ironical mockery of their way of speaking.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He spoke as the rest of the prophets had spoken, but ironically: Go, and prosper ... with such an air and pronunciation as plainly showed he spoke it by way of derision
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “The earth was split”: the crowd's shout of joy
notes.about: As Solomon comes up from his anointing, the crowd's flutes and shouts are so loud that the earth is said to split by the sound. The words say more than is meant literally, to show how loud and great the people's joy was.

figure.name: Hyperbole
figure.words: the earth was split by the sound
figure.means: the people's great joy: the loud noise of their shouts and flutes, as if the ground shook with it

original.note: In Hebrew the verb is baqa, to burst in pieces, the word 2 Chronicles 25:12 uses of men dashed to pieces.

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the earth nearly burst with the shouting and calls the verb, to burst in pieces, a hyperbolical expression for quaking. Joseph Benson calls the words a hyperbolical expression for the very loud noise of the shouts and pipes; Adam Clarke likens them to our saying that cries rend the air. E. W. Bullinger lists them under Hyperbole, of the people leaping for joy.
notes.limit: The writers read the picture in different ways: the ground quaking under the shouting, the loudness of the noise, or the people leaping for joy.

cites.quote: with flutes and loud acclamation, so that the earth nearly burst with their shouting. ... "to burst in pieces" (as in Ch2 25:12 ), is a hyperbolical expression for quaking.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: So that the earth rent An hyperbolical expression, to signify the very loud noise which the people made with their shouts and their pipes.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: The earth rent - We use a similar expression in precisely the same sense: They rent the air with their cries.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: “So that the earth rent with the sound of them.” A hyperbolical description of their jumping and leaping for joy.

notes.about: Omri is named first and last, and Tibni between: Omri's followers prove stronger than Tibni's, then Tibni dies and Omri becomes king.

lines.words: But the followers of Omri proved stronger
than those of Tibni son of Ginath.

notes.evidence: Boys finds the arrangement here turning on two men, with Omri in the two parts he marks a and Tibni in the two he marks b. In the verse, Omri's parts come first and last, and Tibni's between.

cites.quote: In other cases, again, we do not find the arrangement turning upon two kinds or classes of persons, but upon two individuals … Omri in a. and a.; Tibni in b. and b.
cites.read: the 1825 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/akeytobookpsalm00boysgoog

notes.short: A saying: no boasting before the battle is won
notes.about: Ben-hadad has sworn that not enough dust will remain of Samaria for each of his men to have a handful. Ahab answers with a short saying, read as a proverb: a man still putting on his armor has not yet won, so he should not boast like one taking it off after the battle.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: The one putting on his armor should not boast like one taking it off.
figure.means: do not boast of victory before the battle is fought and won

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, among sayings first found in Scripture that have since passed into general use, and says it has come down to later ages as a proverb with many applications. Clarke says it was no doubt a proverbial way of speaking. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) says Ahab's reply has the air of a proverb, the kind Eastern peoples love to answer a foe with.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whether the saying was already in use when Ahab spoke or first appears here and passed into common use later; one says only that the reply sounds like a proverb.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 761
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... This also has come down to, and is used by posterity as a proverb, full of meaning, and with many applications
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Let not him that girdeth on - This was no doubt a proverbial mode of expression.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Ahab's reply has the air of a proverb, with which Orientals always love to answer a foe.

notes.short: A soldier's lost captive pictures Ahab's own deed
notes.about: A wounded prophet in disguise tells King Ahab that he let a captive slip away while on guard. Ahab answers that the man has pronounced his own sentence. Then the prophet shows who he is: Ahab had let go Ben-hadad, the man God had devoted to destruction, and the same sentence falls on Ahab.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Your servant had marched out into the middle of the battle
figure.means: Ahab himself, who had let Ben-hadad go, the man God had devoted to destruction, so that Ahab's sentence on the soldier was his own

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry says the prophet reproved Ahab by a parable, as Nathan did David, charging himself with Ahab's crime in sparing Ben-hadad. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says he did as Nathan had done, by a symbolic action that led the king to sentence himself. Poole calls the story a parable that made the king condemn himself; Robert Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) likens it to Nathan's parable.

cites.quote: This prophet designed to reprove Ahab by a parable, that he might oblige him to condemn himself, as Nathan and the woman of Tekoa did David ... he made his application to the king in a story wherein he charged himself with such a crime as the king was now guilty of in sparing Ben-hadad
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: to announce to the king that God would punish him for letting Benhadad go, and to do this, as Nathan had formerly done in the case of David ... by means of a symbolical action, whereby the king was led to pronounce sentence upon himself.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: this following relation is not an untruth, but a parable ... wherein an obscure prophet was to speak to a great king ... who by this artifice is made to condemn himself before he was aware of it, and so forced to receive the prophet’s just sentence
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/1_kings/20.htm

cites.quote: The prophet found a willing assistant, and then, waiting for Ahab, leads the king unconsciously, in the parabolic manner of Nathan ... to pronounce his own doom
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)
